Record f0-area-candidates, written 2026-11-25T18:51:13Z.

  • Substations: of the 128 OpenStreetMap substations on that land (187 were fetched for the whole box), 20 are tagged substation=traction (rail traction substations); these are not counted by the pass rule, the score or the figure. 30 carry no substation=* tag at all; they are not known to be rail and are counted. Outlines closer than 150 m are one site: 108 outlines that are not rail make 90 sites, of which 28 have an outline within 100 m of flooding on the city's 2.13 in/hr map. Windows passing the rule: 6 counting sites, 15 counting outlines that are not rail, 25 counting every outline.

Checks. Counts in 16 km² windows on a 500 m step. A window is a candidate when at least 60% of it is land of Brooklyn or Queens, by the city's 2020 neighbourhood outlines, and only marks, sensors, substations and reports on that land (within 50 m) are counted. The Jamaica Bay watershed boundary was not used. The Limited Flood map could not be read and is not counted.

SFINCS and HydroMT-SFINCS stood up; toy model timed at three sizes

F0 pass

Record f0-solver-timing, written 2026-11-25T19:08:07Z.

  • Wall time is measured around 'docker run' and includes container start.
  • Parallel batches: the runs start together; batch wall time is the longest run.
  • Every toy value is a placeholder [P]; the toy exists to time the solver.
  • Catalogue size: plan F0's rule sets 150 runs, since one run at 600,000 cells is estimated at 425 s, under 600 s. Those 150 runs take about 17.7 hours of solver time one after another on this machine, more than the 12 hours used as a yardstick (about 101 runs fit in 12 hours). Running in parallel does not shorten it: 2 runs at once gave 0.96 times the throughput of runs one after another; 4 runs at once gave 0.89 times the throughput of runs one after another. Real terrain with buildings may need a smaller time step than the toy, which would make each run longer.

Assets of the study area: substations and buildings in one table

F1 not judged

Record f1-assets, written 2026-11-25T22:06:01Z.

  • Substation values are placeholders [P] bracketed by two published figures for other substations (values.toml); the mid is their geometric mean. They are in the lab_value_* columns with tag P only: BuildingTIV, an OED column, is empty for them. Building values are the inventory's depreciated replacement value [S], August 2025 prices, not 2026 dollars.
  • Building value rule: the SUM of val_struct over every inventory record assigned to the building (inside its footprint, or the nearest footprint within 15 m), because the publisher states that stacked structures are several records on one footprint with the value divided among them (facts file usace-national-structure-inventory, fact known_limits). lab_inventory_points is the number of records summed; lab_occupancy_all lists their distinct occupancy classes; lab_occupancy_hazus, lab_foundation_type, NumberOfStoreys and lab_nsi_id are those of the record of largest value. Total by this rule 48,370,640,327 USD; keeping only the largest record gave 41,195,360,529 USD. Of the 2,480 buildings with several records, 1,923 have records that all carry one real inventory footprint id (ftprntid, not none_...), worth 23,912,919,661 USD summed; 557 do not (different or none_ ids), so their grouping rests on our spatial attribution, worth 7,456,042,297 USD summed. A record attributed by position may belong to a neighbour, so the second group is the less certain part of the sum.
  • Subgrade: where the table's grade is 0 (not measured) its subgrade flag is a default, so lab_subgrade is left empty there (322 buildings). Where the table's notes say the property was not visible, its guidance does not record whether the grade or the floor was the estimated value: those rows have ground source 'z_grade (grade or floor estimated)', and their first-floor height carries the same doubt.
  • Substation grouping, as the code applies it: outlines with the same name within 300 m of each other are one asset; outlines with no name are grouped among themselves within 150 m; outlines with different names are never merged, however close; rail traction substations are left out. Centroid distances between the four named Con Edison assets, metres: S-250386730 Water Street Substation to S-339711332 Farragut Substation: 281.2; S-250386730 Water Street Substation to S-383102724 Hudson Avenue Substation: 62.4; S-250386730 Water Street Substation to S-383110539 Plymouth Substation: 147.4; S-339711332 Farragut Substation to S-383102724 Hudson Avenue Substation: 251.9; S-339711332 Farragut Substation to S-383110539 Plymouth Substation: 139.5; S-383102724 Hudson Avenue Substation to S-383110539 Plymouth Substation: 136.2. Assets this close would be reached by the same water.
  • Customers served (FD7): no public figure per substation exists, so lab_customers_served and lab_customers_tag are empty. A placeholder would need the population of the study area by census block (2020), a service-area rule assigning each block to one substation (for example the nearest area substation, which ignores the real feeder network), and a persons-per-customer ratio from a stated source; none of it is computed here.
  • terrain from flood_lab.terrain.ground_elevation.
  • The table has no column for: footprint area, the operator, location and building tags of a substation; they are in this record and in the cache file assets/buildings_detail.csv. The estimated-grade note is carried in lab_ground_elev_source as 'z_grade (grade or floor estimated)'.

Software: crc-framework 1.0.0, crc-sdk 1.0.0, python 3.12.11

Terrain: 1 m lidar, 5 m grid, water, deep patches and a check on datum and units

F1 pass

Record f1-terrain, written 2026-11-25T21:24:52Z.

  • hillshade.png: shading exaggerates nothing but hides absolute height; water is the F1 rule, not a mapped shoreline; the study area outline comes from census-based neighbourhood outlines simplified to 1 m.
  • elevation.png: the colour scale is fixed at -2 to 30 m, so the river (flat -1.62 m) and the deep patches (below -5 m) share the bottom colour; the black line is the outline of the land in the city's neighbourhood areas, not a surveyed shoreline.
  • footprint_difference.png: 17728 footprints; the city's ground elevation is a lowest-adjacent-grade value in feet whose accuracy varies by source and is not independent of lidar for every footprint; the terrain side is the median of 1 m pixels 1 to 3 m outside the footprint, leaving out water and other footprints; values beyond +-3 m are drawn in the end bins (28 of them). It tests units and vertical datum; a horizontal offset of about 1 m would barely show in it.
  • deep_patches.png: patches are 8-connected pixels below -5 m; what they are is read from shape and position, not from a map of the place (see the notes on the patches).
  • subgrid_range.png: maximum minus minimum of the 25 pixels of 1 m in each 5 m cell, on bare earth; walls and buildings are not in the terrain, so the relief a cell hides in the city is larger than shown. Scale fixed at 0 to 5 m.
  • Horizontal datum: PROJ 9.8.1 (network off) uses 'Inverse of UTM zone 18N + NAD83 to WGS 84 (1) + UTM zone 18N' between EPSG:26918 and EPSG:32618, a null operation (largest shift at the corners and centre 1.15e-04 m); the more accurate operations need grids that are not installed. The terrain is therefore cut on its own pixel grid and relabelled, not resampled. Its position carries the NAD83-to-WGS84 difference: 1.1 m here (-0.403 m east, 1.024 m north from NAD83 to WGS 84 (G1762) at epoch 2013.948, by 'Conversion from NAD83(2011) (geog2D) to NAD83(2011) (geocentric) + Inverse of IT...', accuracy 0.01 m), so a point labelled (x, y) on the terrain lies about that far from the WGS84 position of the same name. The tile's NAD83 is assumed to be NAD83(2011).
  • Deep patch 1: 15274 m², minimum -13.49 m, median -12.84 m, at 40.70253 N 73.97067 W, near 'Brooklyn Navy Yard' (Brooklyn); 1% of its pixels inside the land outlines, 1% in the study area; fits a rectangle 330.0 m by 50.1 m filled to 92%; 83% of its pixels lie within 0.5 m of its 10th percentile (a flat floor); 0% of the pixels touching it are flattened water; their median is -0.42 m.
  • Deep patch 2: 15633 m², minimum -13.31 m, median -12.84 m, at 40.70150 N 73.97101 W, near 'Brooklyn Navy Yard' (Brooklyn); 8% of its pixels inside the land outlines, 8% in the study area; fits a rectangle 339.3 m by 49.5 m filled to 93%; 86% of its pixels lie within 0.5 m of its 10th percentile (a flat floor); 0% of the pixels touching it are flattened water; their median is -0.29 m.
  • Deep patch 3: 1939 m², minimum -8.14 m, median -7.33 m, at 40.70140 N 73.97601 W, near 'Brooklyn Navy Yard' (Brooklyn); 100% of its pixels inside the land outlines, 100% in the study area; fits a rectangle 107.4 m by 21.6 m filled to 84%; 44% of its pixels lie within 0.5 m of its 10th percentile (a flat floor); 0% of the pixels touching it are flattened water; their median is -4.27 m.
  • Deep patches, reading. Evidence: every patch lies in or beside the outline named Brooklyn Navy Yard, is a near-rectangle (fill of its rectangle above), mostly with a flat floor, and no flattened-water pixel touches it, so a rim of terrain closes it off from the flattened river. The two large ones lie in slips that the city's outlines leave out of the land. Guess, not checked against a map or record of the yard: they are the yard's dry docks, drained when the lidar was flown; the two of about 330 m by 50 m look like the two largest docks, the small one on land like an older, smaller dock. For the flood model they are pits 7 to 13 m deep: the parts inside the study area (see share_in_study_area) would hold water that in reality may be held out by a gate, or be already filled; F3 decides how to treat them.
  • Sub-grid tables (HydroMT-SFINCS 2.0.0): 640000 active cells of 640000, 215 MB, 45.4 s with 40.1 s for the tables, peak memory 0.98 GiB. Grid only: no forcing, no boundary, no run; roughness uniform [P]. The tables' cell minimum is not the minimum of the 25 pixels of 1 m: 54% of cells agree within 0.01 m and 98.2% within 0.1 m (percentiles 0, 1, 50, 99, 100 of the difference: -4.68, -0.14, -0.00, +0.04, +1.14 m); HydroMT samples the terrain at 0.5 m, and how it interpolates was not read from its code.

Checks. Bare-earth terrain from lidar flown 2013-08-06 to 2014-04-21 (USGS 3DEP 1 m, project NY_CMPG_2013): buildings, grading and shoreline changes since then are absent, and the river is a flat surface at -1.62 m, not a depth. Every threshold and colour scale is a placeholder [P]. Figures: hillshade.png, elevation.png, footprint_difference.png, deep_patches.png, subgrid_range.png; the limit of each is in the notes below.

City flood maps: loader against the second reader, and the CRC layer

F2 pass

Record second-reader-nyc-stormwater-flood-maps, written 2026-11-25T23:42:50Z.

  • The Limited Flood map is different: both readers open the same export, made through ESRI's library (tools/flood/limited_flood_map). The second reader therefore recomputes only the step from that export to the grid. The step from the publisher's geodatabase to the export rests on the export's own proof: the same route reproduces the Moderate map as GDAL reads it. The export takes vertices only; the map's one curved segment lies outside the study square (F2 report, section 1).
  • Both readers also share the choice of grid frame (EPSG:2263 to EPSG:26918, read as the project grid), which is the project's convention and not something a comparison of the two can test.
  • The square holds water and Manhattan as well as the study area; cell counts are for the whole 4 km square.

Checks. Two readers that agree show the loader does what its statement says. For three scenarios both open the publisher's geodatabase with the same GDAL driver, the only open reader of that format, so a fault in that driver would be shared.

F3 fail

Record f3-model, written 2026-11-26T20:32:03Z.

  • calibration_curve.png: Modelled area per city class (4 in to 1 ft, 1 ft and over) on the compared cells against the constant loss rate, one marker per calibration run, with the city map's area as a dashed line; below, the critical success index for wet (4 in or more) with model patches under a quarter acre removed (filtered) and without (raw), and for the deep class; green: the frozen value. Limit: 12 runs, each 1 h of uniform rain on the whole square; the city's maps come from another model, so a match is agreement with that model, not with observed flooding.
  • hit_miss.png: Hit, miss and false alarm per compared cell at the frozen loss rate, wet meaning 4 in or more, model patches under a quarter acre removed; grey: compared and dry in both; white: not compared (outside the study area, under a building footprint, a filled pit or water). Limit: a cell takes the city's class at its centre; a shift of one cell between the two maps counts as both a miss and a false alarm.
  • water_balance.png: Rain, losses (the constant loss rate), change in storage (change in water volume) and boundary outflow (net outflow through the four edge cross-sections) per run, thousand m³, over the cells inside the boundary cells; the residual share of the rain is printed above. Limit: the fluxes are the solver's own outputs, so the balance tests their consistency (continuity), not that the rain or the losses are right.
  • replays.png: Maximum inundation depth at cell centres for each replay on the compared cells of the study area, in three classes; red: substation sites with the depth exceeded on 25 m² of their open ground; right: the radar rain each run was forced with, mean over the 4 km square per step. Limit: radar rain at about 1 km cells, held uniform within each cell and hour; no sewer network, only the constant loss rate; an outflow boundary on land, so no run-on from the contributing area outside the square.
  • atlas14.png: NOAA Atlas 14 60-minute depth at the study-area centre against return period, partial duration and annual maximum series, with their 90% bounds, and the three map intensities held for one hour. Limit: a point estimate for a 4 km area; the city's storm shape and duration are not a 60-minute block, so a placement is a reading, not the return period of the map.
  • sensitivity.png: Change in modelled area at 4 in or more (filtered) and in CSI wet against the frozen run of the same scenario, for other durations at the same intensity and other water levels at the water-level boundary. Limit: one run per setting, at the frozen loss rate only.
  • Run folders present but not named in the freeze file: lim_q20.oldbase, mod_q20.oldbase.

Table atlas14_placement

Table atlas14_placement. F3 solver model: constant loss rate (the drainage allowance) frozen at 30 mm/h [P] (2026-11-26); 20 of 20 named runs finished. Calibrated on the city's two current-sea-level maps (limited 1.77 in/h, moderate 2.13 in/h); the 3.66 in/h run is a check against a 2080 map. Every number comes from the run folders, the city maps and the cache files listed as inputs. Captions: calibration_curve.png: Modelled area per city class (4 in to 1 ft, 1 ft and over) on the compared cells against the constant loss rate, one marker per calibration run, with the city map's area as a dashed line; below, the critical success index for wet (4 in or more) with model patches under a quarter acre removed (filtered) and without (raw), and for the deep class; green: the frozen value. Limit: 12 runs, each 1 h of uniform rain on the whole square; the city's maps come from another model, so a match is agreement with that model, not with observed flooding. hit_miss.png: Hit, miss and false alarm per compared cell at the frozen loss rate, wet meaning 4 in or more, model patches under a quarter acre removed; grey: compared and dry in both; white: not compared (outside the study area, under a building footprint, a filled pit or water). Limit: a cell takes the city's class at its centre; a shift of one cell between the two maps counts as both a miss and a false alarm. water_balance.png: Rain, losses (the constant loss rate), change in storage (change in water volume) and boundary outflow (net outflow through the four edge cross-sections) per run, thousand m³, over the cells inside the boundary cells; the residual share of the rain is printed above. Limit: the fluxes are the solver's own outputs, so the balance tests their consistency (continuity), not that the rain or the losses are right. replays.png: Maximum inundation depth at cell centres for each replay on the compared cells of the study area, in three classes; red: substation sites with the depth exceeded on 25 m² of their open ground; right: the radar rain each run was forced with, mean over the 4 km square per step. Limit: radar rain at about 1 km cells, held uniform within each cell and hour; no sewer network, only the constant loss rate; an outflow boundary on land, so no run-on from the contributing area outside the square. atlas14.png: NOAA Atlas 14 60-minute depth at the study-area centre against return period, partial duration and annual maximum series, with their 90% bounds, and the three map intensities held for one hour. Limit: a point estimate for a 4 km area; the city's storm shape and duration are not a 60-minute block, so a placement is a reading, not the return period of the map. sensitivity.png: Change in modelled area at 4 in or more (filtered) and in CSI wet against the frozen run of the same scenario, for other durations at the same intensity and other water levels at the water-level boundary. Limit: one run per setting, at the frozen loss rate only.

Table captions

Table captions. F3 solver model: constant loss rate (the drainage allowance) frozen at 30 mm/h [P] (2026-11-26); 20 of 20 named runs finished. Calibrated on the city's two current-sea-level maps (limited 1.77 in/h, moderate 2.13 in/h); the 3.66 in/h run is a check against a 2080 map. Every number comes from the run folders, the city maps and the cache files listed as inputs. Captions: calibration_curve.png: Modelled area per city class (4 in to 1 ft, 1 ft and over) on the compared cells against the constant loss rate, one marker per calibration run, with the city map's area as a dashed line; below, the critical success index for wet (4 in or more) with model patches under a quarter acre removed (filtered) and without (raw), and for the deep class; green: the frozen value. Limit: 12 runs, each 1 h of uniform rain on the whole square; the city's maps come from another model, so a match is agreement with that model, not with observed flooding. hit_miss.png: Hit, miss and false alarm per compared cell at the frozen loss rate, wet meaning 4 in or more, model patches under a quarter acre removed; grey: compared and dry in both; white: not compared (outside the study area, under a building footprint, a filled pit or water). Limit: a cell takes the city's class at its centre; a shift of one cell between the two maps counts as both a miss and a false alarm. water_balance.png: Rain, losses (the constant loss rate), change in storage (change in water volume) and boundary outflow (net outflow through the four edge cross-sections) per run, thousand m³, over the cells inside the boundary cells; the residual share of the rain is printed above. Limit: the fluxes are the solver's own outputs, so the balance tests their consistency (continuity), not that the rain or the losses are right. replays.png: Maximum inundation depth at cell centres for each replay on the compared cells of the study area, in three classes; red: substation sites with the depth exceeded on 25 m² of their open ground; right: the radar rain each run was forced with, mean over the 4 km square per step. Limit: radar rain at about 1 km cells, held uniform within each cell and hour; no sewer network, only the constant loss rate; an outflow boundary on land, so no run-on from the contributing area outside the square. atlas14.png: NOAA Atlas 14 60-minute depth at the study-area centre against return period, partial duration and annual maximum series, with their 90% bounds, and the three map intensities held for one hour. Limit: a point estimate for a 4 km area; the city's storm shape and duration are not a 60-minute block, so a placement is a reading, not the return period of the map. sensitivity.png: Change in modelled area at 4 in or more (filtered) and in CSI wet against the frozen run of the same scenario, for other durations at the same intensity and other water levels at the water-level boundary. Limit: one run per setting, at the frozen loss rate only.

Table runs

Table runs. F3 solver model: constant loss rate (the drainage allowance) frozen at 30 mm/h [P] (2026-11-26); 20 of 20 named runs finished. Calibrated on the city's two current-sea-level maps (limited 1.77 in/h, moderate 2.13 in/h); the 3.66 in/h run is a check against a 2080 map. Every number comes from the run folders, the city maps and the cache files listed as inputs. Captions: calibration_curve.png: Modelled area per city class (4 in to 1 ft, 1 ft and over) on the compared cells against the constant loss rate, one marker per calibration run, with the city map's area as a dashed line; below, the critical success index for wet (4 in or more) with model patches under a quarter acre removed (filtered) and without (raw), and for the deep class; green: the frozen value. Limit: 12 runs, each 1 h of uniform rain on the whole square; the city's maps come from another model, so a match is agreement with that model, not with observed flooding. hit_miss.png: Hit, miss and false alarm per compared cell at the frozen loss rate, wet meaning 4 in or more, model patches under a quarter acre removed; grey: compared and dry in both; white: not compared (outside the study area, under a building footprint, a filled pit or water). Limit: a cell takes the city's class at its centre; a shift of one cell between the two maps counts as both a miss and a false alarm. water_balance.png: Rain, losses (the constant loss rate), change in storage (change in water volume) and boundary outflow (net outflow through the four edge cross-sections) per run, thousand m³, over the cells inside the boundary cells; the residual share of the rain is printed above. Limit: the fluxes are the solver's own outputs, so the balance tests their consistency (continuity), not that the rain or the losses are right. replays.png: Maximum inundation depth at cell centres for each replay on the compared cells of the study area, in three classes; red: substation sites with the depth exceeded on 25 m² of their open ground; right: the radar rain each run was forced with, mean over the 4 km square per step. Limit: radar rain at about 1 km cells, held uniform within each cell and hour; no sewer network, only the constant loss rate; an outflow boundary on land, so no run-on from the contributing area outside the square. atlas14.png: NOAA Atlas 14 60-minute depth at the study-area centre against return period, partial duration and annual maximum series, with their 90% bounds, and the three map intensities held for one hour. Limit: a point estimate for a 4 km area; the city's storm shape and duration are not a 60-minute block, so a placement is a reading, not the return period of the map. sensitivity.png: Change in modelled area at 4 in or more (filtered) and in CSI wet against the frozen run of the same scenario, for other durations at the same intensity and other water levels at the water-level boundary. Limit: one run per setting, at the frozen loss rate only.

Table runs_not_run

Table runs_not_run. F3 solver model: constant loss rate (the drainage allowance) frozen at 30 mm/h [P] (2026-11-26); 20 of 20 named runs finished. Calibrated on the city's two current-sea-level maps (limited 1.77 in/h, moderate 2.13 in/h); the 3.66 in/h run is a check against a 2080 map. Every number comes from the run folders, the city maps and the cache files listed as inputs. Captions: calibration_curve.png: Modelled area per city class (4 in to 1 ft, 1 ft and over) on the compared cells against the constant loss rate, one marker per calibration run, with the city map's area as a dashed line; below, the critical success index for wet (4 in or more) with model patches under a quarter acre removed (filtered) and without (raw), and for the deep class; green: the frozen value. Limit: 12 runs, each 1 h of uniform rain on the whole square; the city's maps come from another model, so a match is agreement with that model, not with observed flooding. hit_miss.png: Hit, miss and false alarm per compared cell at the frozen loss rate, wet meaning 4 in or more, model patches under a quarter acre removed; grey: compared and dry in both; white: not compared (outside the study area, under a building footprint, a filled pit or water). Limit: a cell takes the city's class at its centre; a shift of one cell between the two maps counts as both a miss and a false alarm. water_balance.png: Rain, losses (the constant loss rate), change in storage (change in water volume) and boundary outflow (net outflow through the four edge cross-sections) per run, thousand m³, over the cells inside the boundary cells; the residual share of the rain is printed above. Limit: the fluxes are the solver's own outputs, so the balance tests their consistency (continuity), not that the rain or the losses are right. replays.png: Maximum inundation depth at cell centres for each replay on the compared cells of the study area, in three classes; red: substation sites with the depth exceeded on 25 m² of their open ground; right: the radar rain each run was forced with, mean over the 4 km square per step. Limit: radar rain at about 1 km cells, held uniform within each cell and hour; no sewer network, only the constant loss rate; an outflow boundary on land, so no run-on from the contributing area outside the square. atlas14.png: NOAA Atlas 14 60-minute depth at the study-area centre against return period, partial duration and annual maximum series, with their 90% bounds, and the three map intensities held for one hour. Limit: a point estimate for a 4 km area; the city's storm shape and duration are not a 60-minute block, so a placement is a reading, not the return period of the map. sensitivity.png: Change in modelled area at 4 in or more (filtered) and in CSI wet against the frozen run of the same scenario, for other durations at the same intensity and other water levels at the water-level boundary. Limit: one run per setting, at the frozen loss rate only.

  • sites_map.png: Hudson Avenue (top) and Farragut (bottom) substations: modelled maximum inundation depth on 1 m pixels in the Moderate map storm (2.13 in/hr for one hour) and the Ida replay. Thick line: the site's fence outline from OpenStreetMap; thin: the other substations of the complex. Red rings: the 25 m² the lead-asset rule reads.   • sites_depth.png: Depth over 25 m² of open ground at the two sites in five storms, ordered by the rain of their peak hour, with the Atlas 14 return period of that hour (partial-duration series, between two tabulated columns, no interpolation). Limit: a storm's return period is not the return period of the depth it causes; the replays' 2- and 3-hour rain may sit in other classes (record table 'storms'); equipment heights are unknown.

F4 fail

Record f4, written 2026-11-26T20:38:45Z.

  • domain.png: 3-hour ratio map (smoothed mean annual maximum over the study area's, AORC 2002-2025) over the download window, domain B, the study box and the 960 storms of the chosen catalogue, each at the centre of the box-sized window of its largest 3-hour rain (RainyDay's storm location).
  • rainfall_frequency.png: 3-hour annual maximum rainfall at the study box: the chosen catalogue (960 storms, M = 1000, T = M / rank), the 240- and 480-storm sensitivities, Atlas 14 AMS 3-hr with its 90% band, and AORC observed box maxima at Weibull plotting positions T = (n + 1) / i. Below the band at 2-10 y: fail, accepted (CH-19).
  • depth_strip.png: Per-cell depth at 10, 100 and 500 years from the catalogue (N = 60 catalogue storms (interim weights), 1000 of 1000 years covered) beside the 1-hour and 3-hour Atlas 14 design storms of the same return periods.
  • buildings_wet.png: Buildings of the study area wet at the wall (0.05 m, 0.3 m) at 100 years: the catalogue (N = 60 catalogue storms (interim weights), 1000 of 1000 years covered; each building's own curve at annual exceedance probability (AEP) 0.01) against each design storm; beside it every design storm with the 5 m cells it wets. Shaded: storms that wet no 5 m cell or whose rain does not exceed the 30 mm/h constant loss rate; since CH-20 and CH-21 (ground never below a cell's lowest sub-grid level) they wet no cell and no building, where before they showed about 2,900 buildings.
  • wet_runs.png: Number of catalogue runs wetting each read 5 m cell (N = 60 catalogue storms (interim weights), 1000 of 1000 years covered).
  • progress.png: Catalogue runs finished per stratum; solver wall time and water-balance residual per finished run (catalogue and design).

Checks. F4 storm catalogue and batch: N = 60 catalogue storms (interim weights), 1000 of 1000 years covered. Depth frequency is empirical (catalogue.depth_at, RainyDay's rank convention), one storm per synthetic year; the largest-rain storm of a year is taken as its worst flood. Grid depth: calibration.run_depth (src/flood_lab/hazard/calibration.py): peak water level less the ground at each 5 m cell's centre 1 m pixel, the ground never below the cell's lowest sub-grid level (CH-20), floored at 0, the definition the constant loss rate was calibrated and FH8 tested on; not read (NaN) where calibration.Frame leaves a cell out: centre pixel in a building footprint, any pixel in a filled pit, centre pixel on mapped water, lowest level below the start water level (CH-16). Whole square, not only the study area. Asset depths: at_assets (1 m pixels; substation lead measure, building wall band). Figures made before the batch completes are rebuilt afterwards (requirements §15).

Numbers. F4 storm catalogue and batch: N = 60 catalogue storms (interim weights), 1000 of 1000 years covered. Depth frequency is empirical (catalogue.depth_at, RainyDay's rank convention), one storm per synthetic year; the largest-rain storm of a year is taken as its worst flood. Grid depth: calibration.run_depth (src/flood_lab/hazard/calibration.py): peak water level less the ground at each 5 m cell's centre 1 m pixel, the ground never below the cell's lowest sub-grid level (CH-20), floored at 0, the definition the constant loss rate was calibrated and FH8 tested on; not read (NaN) where calibration.Frame leaves a cell out: centre pixel in a building footprint, any pixel in a filled pit, centre pixel on mapped water, lowest level below the start water level (CH-16). Whole square, not only the study area. Asset depths: at_assets (1 m pixels; substation lead measure, building wall band). Figures made before the batch completes are rebuilt afterwards (requirements §15).

 "buildings_wet.png": "Buildings of the study area wet at the wall (0.05 m, 0.3 m) at 100 years: the catalogue (N = 60 catalogue storms (interim weights), 1000 of 1000 years covered; each building's own curve at annual exceedance probability (AEP) 0.01) against each design storm; beside it every design storm with the 5 m cells it wets. Table catalogue_wet_cells_005

Table catalogue_wet_cells_005. F4 storm catalogue and batch: N = 60 catalogue storms (interim weights), 1000 of 1000 years covered. Depth frequency is empirical (catalogue.depth_at, RainyDay's rank convention), one storm per synthetic year; the largest-rain storm of a year is taken as its worst flood. Grid depth: calibration.run_depth (src/flood_lab/hazard/calibration.py): peak water level less the ground at each 5 m cell's centre 1 m pixel, the ground never below the cell's lowest sub-grid level (CH-20), floored at 0, the definition the constant loss rate was calibrated and FH8 tested on; not read (NaN) where calibration.Frame leaves a cell out: centre pixel in a building footprint, any pixel in a filled pit, centre pixel on mapped water, lowest level below the start water level (CH-16). Whole square, not only the study area. Asset depths: at_assets (1 m pixels; substation lead measure, building wall band). Figures made before the batch completes are rebuilt afterwards (requirements §15).

Validation against observations: Ida high-water marks and FloodNet sensors

F5 not judged

Record f5, written 2026-11-26T17:43:53Z.

  • Published comparison: The 0.20 m is the error of a model calibrated on those 8 marks: a fitted figure, not an independent test. 0.40 m is the same model before calibration. (Kasaei et al. 2025, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 29:2043).
  • Vertical datum: zsmax is the solver's water level in metres NAVD88, the datum of the model terrain (USGS 3DEP 1 m, NAVD88) and of the water-level boundary (0 m NAVD88); the marks are surveyed in NAVD88 (feet, converted with 0.3048).
  • Marks: horizontal positions are phone or map fixes (WGS84 from digital map), so a mark's 1 m pixel may be a few metres off; the deepest modelled depth within 10 m is given beside the pixel's for that reason, not used in the statistics.
  • The cached FloodNet events table carries each event's depth profile (flood_profile_depth_inches, flood_profile_time_secs); the panels draw it as published. Its peak is the loader's max_depth_inches.
  • marks_scatter.png: Ida replay (frozen F3 model, constant loss rate 30 mm/h) against the 11 USGS high-water marks in the square (6 sites). Left: inundation depth at the mark's 1 m pixel (modelled water level less ground level, ground never below the cell's lowest sub-grid level) against the surveyed height above ground. Right: modelled peak water level of the 5 m cell against the surveyed mark elevation, NAVD88. Grey band: ±0.20 m, the error Kasaei et al. 2025 report after calibrating on 8 marks (a fitted figure, not an independent test; 0.40 m before calibration). Limit: marks are phone fixes (positions to a few metres) and were surveyed weeks later.
  • sensors.png: FloodNet sensors in the square in service on each storm day: measured depth through each event as published (times UTC), the modelled peak at the sensor's pixel (solid) and the deepest modelled depth on open ground within 10 m (dashed; sensor positions are approximate). Limit: the model gives a peak, not a time series, here.
  • error_map.png: Modelled maximum inundation depth on read open ground with the depth error, model less observed, at each mark (circles, Ida) and sensor (squares; thick edge: in service, none recorded).

Checks. F5 first part (FV1, FV2, FV4; FV3 and FV5 later). Model against observations is reported, not judged. The depth error at the marks (0.21 m RMSE) is within 0.5 m [P]; FV4's statement is not required. No parameter is changed (FV4).

{
 "error_map.png": "Modelled maximum inundation depth on read open ground with the depth error, model less observed, at each mark (circles, Ida) and sensor (squares; thick edge: in service, none recorded).",
 "marks_scatter.png": "Ida replay (frozen F3 model, constant loss rate 30 mm/h) against the 11 USGS high-water marks in the square (6 sites). Left: inundation depth at the mark's 1 m pixel (modelled water level less ground level, ground never below the cell's lowest sub-grid level) against the surveyed height above ground. Right: modelled peak water level of the 5 m cell against the surveyed mark elevation, NAVD88. Grey band: ±0.20 m, the error Kasaei et al. 2025 report after calibrating on 8 marks (a fitted figure, not an independent test; 0.40 m before calibration). Limit: marks are phone fixes (positions to a few metres) and were surveyed weeks later.",
 "sensors.png": "FloodNet sensors in the square in service on each storm day: measured depth through each event as published (times UTC), the modelled peak at the sensor's pixel (solid) and the deepest modelled depth on open ground within 10 m (dashed; sensor positions are approximate). Limit: the model gives a peak, not a time series, here."
}

Software: crc-framework 1.0.0, crc-sdk 1.0.0, geopandas 1.2.0, matplotlib 3.11.2, numpy 2.5.4, pyproj 3.8.0, python 3.12.11, rasterio 1.5.1

Jamaica Bay map overlap (FV3) and who saw the flood (FV5)

F5 not judged

Record f5-who-saw, written 2026-11-27T01:51:01Z.

  • Storm Events clock: every New York City row says EST-5; times are turned into UTC and then into the New York wall clock before a day is matched (facts noaa-storm-events, time_zone).
  • 311: created_date has no zone; read as the New York wall clock as written.
  • Sightings (observations.sightings) are the lab's grouping, refining the facts row's 'count both': twin rows are one request, and reports close in place and time are one sighting with every member kept. Change entry CH-24 is proposed, not entered.
  • who_saw_counts.png: Counts inside the model square for each source and storm. Dark bar: the main count (Groundsource places centred in the square; Storm Events flood events with a point in it; 311 flooding-related requests with twin rows of the two naming schemes paired; FloodNet sensors that recorded an event; USGS marks). Light bar: the context (places touching the square; flood events of the square's counties and zones; 311 rows of both schemes; sensors in service; mark sites). Windows: Ida 1 and 2 Sep 2021, the other storm 29 Sep 2023, each source by its own date rule (record, RULES). Counts are reported, not judged: a source with no entry is not evidence of no flood.
  • who_saw_map_ida_2021.png: Ida, 1-2 Sep 2021: who saw the flood inside the model square. Background: the frozen F3 replay of this storm, maximum inundation depth from 0.05 m (for orientation only; nothing is compared). Purple dots: 311 flooding-related requests, a twin pair drawn once. Black rings: sightings of more than one report (observations.sightings: within 50 m and 12 h, chained), the number of reports beside rings of three or more. Green squares: FloodNet sensors in service (filled: recorded an event). Black diamonds: USGS marks. Orange outlines: Groundsource places of the storm days, solid when centred in the square, dashed when within 500 m and no larger than the square (larger places, such as a borough, are counted but not drawn). Dotted red: the hull of the points of a Storm Events event with a point in the square.
  • who_saw_map_sep29_2023.png: 29 Sep 2023: who saw the flood inside the model square. Background: the frozen F3 replay of this storm, maximum inundation depth from 0.05 m (for orientation only; nothing is compared). Purple dots: 311 flooding-related requests, a twin pair drawn once. Black rings: sightings of more than one report (observations.sightings: within 50 m and 12 h, chained), the number of reports beside rings of three or more. Green squares: FloodNet sensors in service (filled: recorded an event). Black diamonds: USGS marks. Orange outlines: Groundsource places of the storm days, solid when centred in the square, dashed when within 500 m and no larger than the square (larger places, such as a borough, are counted but not drawn). Dotted red: the hull of the points of a Storm Events event with a point in the square.
  • late_calls.png: Flooding-related 311 requests per day inside the square (twin rows paired), four weeks each side of each storm. Dark: the storm days; light purple: the two days after; grey: dry days, the baseline (GHCN-Daily rain below 1.0 mm at Central Park, LaGuardia and JFK on the day and the 2 days before, other than the storm and the 7 days after); pale: other days. Dashed line: baseline mean; dotted: baseline maximum.
  • jamaica_bay_overlap.png: The Jamaica Bay Ida depth map (Kasaei et al. 2025, Mendeley doi:10.17632/hs2zt6ngwd.1, CC BY 4.0; points of the published shapefile, coloured by flood_dept, metres) within 3.5 km of the model square, with the shortest distance between them. Shown with credit; not changed except for the projection to EPSG:32618.

 "floodnet": {
  "inside": "the sensor table's position, projected to EPSG:32618, lies in the square",
  "window": "context: sensors in service on a storm day (installed on or before it, not removed before it); main count: sensors with an event whose start (GMT) falls on a storm day on the New York clock"
 },
 "groundsource": {
  "inside": "main count: the place polygon's centroid lies in the square; context: the polygon intersects the square (the polygon is the named place, not the flood)",
  "window": "a row whose start_date to end_date range (as published: days, no time of day, no zone) holds one of the storm's days"
 },
 "nyc_311": {
  "inside": "latitude and longitude, projected to EPSG:32618, fall in the square; requests with no location cannot be placed and are counted apart for the two boroughs",
  "window": "created_date (a floating time stamp, read as the New York wall clock as written) falls on one of the storm's days"
 },
 "storm_events": {
  "inside": "main count: the begin point, end point or a point of the locations file lies in the square; context: every flood event of the square's counties (Kings, New York) and NWS zones (75 Kings (Brooklyn), 72 New York (Manhattan)), county and zone events both read",
  "window": "the event's begin to end, turned from its CZ_TIMEZONE clock (EST-5 for every New York City row, also in September) to UTC and then to the New York wall clock, holds one of the storm's days"
 },
 "usgs_marks": {
  "inside": "the mark's position, projected to EPSG:32618, lies in the square",
  "window": "the survey of Ida (ScienceBase item 618975c8d34ec04fc9c5a049); no date matching. The cache holds no survey for 29 Sep 2023; whether USGS surveyed marks for that storm was not checked"
 }
}

{
 "area_reports": "Groundsource places (centred in the square) and Storm Events events (with a point in the square) name an area, not a spot: they join no sighting and link none; each sighting lists the area reports whose shape holds a member (Groundsource: the place polygon over the storm days; Storm Events: the hull of the event's points over its begin to end), with windows within 12 h",
 "duplicates": "the strict case, applied first: 311 twin rows of one request (nyc_311.twins = sightings.duplicate_pairs: other scheme, same kind, within 600 s, same address or within 25 m)",
 "near": "two observations within 50 m [P] and with time windows within 12 h [P] of each other; any source, any kind",
 "observation": "one report of water at a place and time: 311 requests (a twin pair is one observation keeping both row ids; time = created_date), FloodNet events at sensors in the square that started on a storm day (time = start to end, New York clock), USGS marks in the square (no time: the whole storm days)",
 "sighting": "observations joined by chains of near pairs (single linkage); every member is kept with its source and row ids; extent = largest distance between two members"
}

DELUGE: Towards Continental-Scale Daily Pluvial Flood Damage Prediction via Interpretable Conditioning on Foundation Model Embeddings (arXiv 2607.16050), section 3.1.1 arXiv (Cornell University); authors Kawakami, Cayan, Liu, Ma, Corringham; facts checked: 5 confirmed, 3 read with no claim, 1 not checked; 8 confirmed, 0 differs, 1 not checked, 3 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FT5. Known biases: The rule was fitted to NFIP claims 2017-2022 in the 100 highest-claim 75 km cells of the conterminous US (about 81% of pluvial claims), which are in the Northeast and Gulf regions; the shares 81.1/12.9/6.0 describe those claims, not New York City alone. AORC rainfall at the claim location is the only judge of a correct date, so claims for non-rain causes (tidal, river) are also dropped or moved.

Facts of DELUGE: Towards Continental-Scale Daily Pluvial Flood Damage Prediction via Interpretable Conditioning on Foundation Model Embeddings (arXiv 2607.16050), section 3.1.1. rule_text furtherconfirmed10 mm threshold on daily maximum hourly AORC rainfall, window d-3 to d+3Confirmed as stated in requirements FT5: step 1 daily maximum of hourly accumulated precipitation from NOAA AORC at the claim location for day d; step 2 keep d if it exceeds 10 mm; step 3 otherwise take the day in d-3..d+3 with the largest such value and move the claim to it if that exceeds 10 mm; step 4 otherwise discard the claim.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.16050
passage
"3.1.1 Temporal Uncertainty Correction. The dateOfLoss field in the NFIP claims data is known to be noisy where reported dates of loss often fail to align with precipitation events in the historical precipitation records. ... To mitigate this noise, we apply the following correction to the dateOfLoss field d: (1) Compute the daily maximum hourly accumulated precipitation from NOAA AORC [21] for day d at the location of the claim. (2) If the daily maximum hourly accumulated precipitation on day d exceeds 10 mm, accept dateOfLoss as reported. (3) Otherwise, search the window d' in {d - 3, ..., d + 3} and select the day with the largest daily maximum hourly precipitation. If this maximum exceeds 10 mm, update dateOfLoss to d'. (4) If no day's daily maximum hourly precipitation in the window exceeds 10 mm, discard the claim as erroneous."
Threshold rationale in the paper: "We adopt 10 mm as a conservative threshold for maximum hourly accumulated precipitation, sitting between two reference points" (FFG about 25.4 mm; AMS heavy precipitation 7.62 mm in one hour). The paper does not say what rainfall location uncertainty (0.1 degree claim position) does to the daily maximum; the rule is applied "at the location of the claim" after the spatial correction of section 3.1.2.

Appendix Table 6 gives the shift distribution in percent: -3: 2.0, -2: 1.9, -1: 5.0, 0: 81.1, +1: 2.0, +2: 1.4, +3: 0.6, discarded: 6.0 (sums to 100.0; the six non-zero shifts sum to 12.9).https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.16050

FloodNet: Street Flooding Events Measured by FloodNet Sensors NYC Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), data from FloodNet (NYU and CUNY), on NYC Open Data; facts confirmed (8 read with no claim); values recomputed by a second reader in F2 (passed); 12 confirmed, 0 differs, 0 not checked, 1 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FS3, FV2, FT1. Known biases: Sensors sit only where the project could mount them (street furniture, mostly over sidewalks), usually above the local low point, so shallow floods and floods in the roadbed below curb height are missed; a sensor offline, not yet installed or retired records nothing, and the tables do not say when a sensor was offline. The network grew from 9 sensors in September 2021 to 68 in September 2023, so a count of sensors with events is mostly a count of where sensors were.

max_depth_inches | number | The maximum flood depth (in inches) measured at the sensor location during the event
flood_start_time | calendar_date | Start time of the measured flood event (i.e., time when flood waters began accumulating beneath sensor, in GMT)
duration_above_4_inches_mins | number | The amount of time during the flood event that measured water depths were equal to or greater than 4 inches.
A flood event is defined as a series of water depth measurements greater than 10 mm; all measured flood events presented here have undergone QC by a member of the FloodNet team.
Depth is as measured under the sensor, not at the lowest point of the street: see sensor table field lowest_point_height_delta_inches. 2 events (Q-davenport-ct-2-07znk0, 2021-01-16 and 2021-02-02) start before the sensor date_installed (2021-03-05).

If the GMT date is used instead, 2021-09-01 has 0 events and 2021-09-02 has the same 5 sensors (Brooklyn 3, Queens 2): the whole Ida rainfall of the evening of 1 September local time falls on 2 September GMT. Counting events whose [start, end] interval overlaps the local day: 2021-09-01 gives the same 5; 2021-09-02 local gives 3 sensors (Brooklyn 1, Queens 2) because three events run past local midnight.

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FS3, FV2, FT1. Known biases: Sensors sit only where the project could mount them (street furniture, mostly over sidewalks), usually above the local low point, so shallow floods and floods in the roadbed below curb height are missed; a sensor offline, not yet installed or retired records nothing, and the tables do not say when a sensor was offline. The network grew from 9 sensors in September 2021 to 68 in September 2023, so a count of sensors with events is mostly a count of where sensors were.

DEFECT in the file: the GeoParquet metadata uses the key "geometry_type" where the specification has "geometry_types"; DuckDB (2.0.1 with spatial) refuses to open the file with "Geoparquet column 'geometry' does not have geometry types". area_km2_meaning furtherconfirmedDocument that area_km2 is the area of the named place, not of the flood.area_km2 is the area of the geometry polygon of the reported place: the documentation says "Area of the reported location polygon". Checked on the file: on a random sample of 30,000 rows, area_km2 equals the geodesic (spheroid) area of the row geometry within 1% in 99.9% of rows (median ratio 1.0000000001). So it is the place, not the flood.https://eartharxiv.org/repository/view/12083/ (Table 2)

The paper also says: "the dataset structure is entity-based rather than meteorology-based. Therefore, a single large-scale meteorological flood may result in multiple separate entries". Place size filter: events with area over 5,000 km2 or diameter over 500 km are discarded (file max area_km2 = 4998.83).
production furtherconfirmedhow the records were producedNews articles (about 7.5 million processed, about 5 million judged by the LLM to report an actual flood) read in 80 languages, translated to English with Cloud Translation, then Gemini extracts flooded places and dates; places are tied to WebRef entities or geocoded with the Google Maps Geocoding API to polygons; same-place reports on the same or consecutive days are merged into one row; places over 5,000 km2 or 500 km across, runs over 7 days and dates before 2000 are dropped.https://eartharxiv.org/repository/view/12083/ (Section 2) and https://research.google/blog/introducing-groundsource-turning-news-reports-into-data-with-gemini/
passage
paper: "In total, approximately 5 million of the 7.5 million processed articles were identified by the LLM as reporting an actual flood event." ; "Entries reporting the exact same location on the same day, or on consecutive days, are concatenated." ; blog: "The system identifies granular locations (neighborhoods and streets) and maps them to standardized spatial polygons using Google Maps Platform."
The paper is "a non-peer-reviewed preprint" and "an unreviewed preprint" (EarthArXiv, March 9, 2026).
precision furtherconfirmedstated precision or error ratesManual review of 400 random rows: 60% +/- 5% (95% CI) Accurate (place polygon and dates both match the article); a further 22% Approximate or Partial, so 82% practically useful; 18% Wrong. Earlier pipeline steps on 125 hand-labelled articles: classification 75% precision, 90% recall; dates 61% precision, 74% recall; places 64% precision, 69% recall. Recall against GDACS floods 2020-2026: 85% to 100% of severe events. Errors are stated not to be i.i.d.; no regional breakdown is given.https://eartharxiv.org/repository/view/12083/ (Section 4.1)
passage
"Based on this manual review, the pipeline achieved a precision of 60% ± 5% (95% CI), representing entries where both the extracted location and dates perfectly matched the source text (the 'Accurate' category). An additional 22% of the entries were classified as either 'Approximate' or 'Partial.' ... The remaining 18% of evaluated entries were classified as 'Wrong' and considered unusable." ; "we report only the global precision metric."
Failure modes named: same place name in several countries or states, date offsets from relative dates ("the past weekend", "last September" imputed as September 1st). The last matters here: 2021-09-01 is the first of a month.

FEMA Hazus flood depth-damage functions and Hazus Inventory Technical Manual FEMA (Hazus); open-source tool repository nhrap-hazus/FAST on GitHub; facts checked: 4 read with no claim, 1 differ, 1 not checked; 4 confirmed, 1 differs, 1 not checked, 3 not applicable

1 fact(s) differ from docs/flood/requirements.md: licence. Under FS6 the stage stops until the requirements are corrected.

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FR2, FR3, FM5. Known biases: FEMA's own pages and documents returned HTTP 403 to the data-source-check client (www.fema.gov), so the Inventory Technical Manual, Table 10-12 and the 4 ft functional depth were NOT read. The current-version statement comes from an Internet Archive copy of FEMA's Hazus page (secondary). The FAST lookup tables are Hazus 4.0 data; the repository is archived by its owner ('no longer receiving updates').

Interruption Cost Estimate (ICE) Calculator 2.x Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and Resource Innovations, Inc. (icecalculator.com); facts checked: 3 confirmed, 4 read with no claim, 2 differ; 7 confirmed, 2 differs, 0 not checked, 2 not applicable

2 fact(s) differ from docs/flood/requirements.md: identifier, reuse_terms. Under FS6 the stage stops until the requirements are corrected.

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FM5. Known biases: Costs are for interruptions up to 24 hours only (long outages are outside the survey-based method); the model is a survey-based econometric model (4,156 residential and 5,287 non-residential responses in 2.2); the underlying equations and coefficients are copyrighted and licensed, not published. The 2.0-versus-2.2 memorandum shows estimates changed between versions.

Facts of Interruption Cost Estimate (ICE) Calculator 2.x. Each fact as read from the primary source on the date shown; claimed is what the requirements say. Facts are not a recomputation of values.

identifierdiffersICE Calculator 2.0 released 2025-04-28, 2.2 in February 2026Release dates from the site's own bundle (main-22UAKSGH.js, version table; JavaScript months are zero-based): interruption.2.0.0 new Date(2025,3,26) = 2025-04-26; interruption.2.1.0 new Date(2025,7,24) = 2025-08-24; interruption.2.2.0 new Date(2026,1,19) = 2026-02-19 ('New interruption cost model based on results from the Phase 1 and Phase 2 surveying activities'); Guam and Puerto Rico models 1.0.0 also 2026-02-19. The LBNL memo says version 2.0 was 'released in April 2025'. So 2.2 in February 2026 is confirmed; the day of 2.0 is 26 April per the site bundle, not 28 April.https://icecalculator.com/main-22UAKSGH.js

duration_limit furtherconfirmed24 hours or lessConfirmed by the FAQ for ICE 2: 'The focus of the updated ICE Calculator is on the costs of power interruptions lasting up to 24 hours.' Survey-based CDFs cannot provide complete information beyond 24 hours (DOE research cited). Exception: Puerto Rico and Guam can be estimated to 30 days (max CAIDI 43,200 minutes). Input bounds in the app: CAIDI max 1440 min, SAIDI max 2160, SAIFI max 100.https://ice-calc-docs.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/documents/FAQs+for+ICE+Calculator+2.pdf
passage
Does the ICE Calculator estimate the cost of power interruptions lasting longer than 24 hours? The focus of the updated ICE Calculator is on the costs of power interruptions lasting up to 24 hours.
reuse_terms furtherdifferswhether the damage-function coefficients may be used offline [V]NOT freely reusable offline. The online tool and its API stay in the public domain; the spreadsheets (the equations and coefficients) are available only under a licensing agreement; LBNL and partners hold copyright on the underlying models. The Phase 1 final report describes the econometric structure (residential: a GLM; non-residential: a Probit plus a GLM) and lists explanatory variables with significance, but no coefficient values were found in its text (grep of 'coefficient' hits only method sections; report not read in full). So a published coefficient set for offline use was not found; calling the API is the permitted route.https://ice-calc-docs.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/documents/FAQs+for+ICE+Calculator+2.pdf

Those equations include both the explanatory variables included in the models and their coefficients. ... Berkeley Lab-and our partners-filed for and received copyright protection from the U.S. government. Users that wish to access the spreadsheets will now need to go through a process to secure a license. As always, access to the online version of the ICE Calculator-and the Application Programming Interface-will remain in the public domain.  ; site: 'Berkeley Lab and our research partners hold a copyright for the underlying models (e.g., the equations) used by the ICE Calculator.'

Post-tropical cyclone Ida (2021) flood map for New York City’s Jamaica Bay watershed Stevens Institute of Technology and co-authors (Kasaei, Orton, Ralston, Warner), via Mendeley Data; facts confirmed (9 read with no claim); 15 confirmed, 0 differs, 0 not checked, 0 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FV3, FH3. Known biases: Jamaica Bay watershed only. A model product (about 50 m grid, no buildings, no explicit sewers, one lumped drain rate), not an observation, calibrated and scored on a handful of high-water marks, so its 0.20 m is an in-sample figure. The 8 or 18 marks behind it are not independent of the USGS set used elsewhere in this study.

rmse_0_20_m furtherconfirmedthe 0.20 m of the published research model [S] (Kasaei et al. 2025, HESS 29:2043, abstract)The abstract says RMSE of 20 cm against high-water marks: same number as 0.20 m. Caveat: the paper validates against seven USGS marks inside its modeled area plus one from the Community Flood Watch Project (eight for Ida); the Mendeley record says "18 locations" for the calibration using two storms (Ida and 29 Sep 2023). The uncalibrated base run (no drain rate) had RMSE 40 cm and mean error 13 cm. Calibrated drain rate 13 mm/h.https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/29/2043/2025/

abstract: "We generate a spatially continuous flood map of Ida with a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 20 cm when compared to high-water marks" ; text: "we reference surveyed high-water marks (HWMs) from the USGS website for the event, finding seven locations within our modeled area; one more HWM is from the Community Flood Watch Project" ; "The calibrated drain rate of 13 mm h −1 from our model" ; Mendeley: "based on a calibration process that utilized two storms and high watermarks at 18 locations."
The 20 cm is in-sample (a calibration error, not an independent test) on very few marks; do not compare a model validated against the full 159 marks to it as if like for like.

Lidar terrain for New York City: USGS 3DEP 1 m DEM and NYC 2017 topobathymetric lidar DEM U.S. Geological Survey (3DEP); City of New York Office of Technology and Innovation (OTI); facts checked: 4 confirmed, 6 read with no claim, 2 differ, 3 not checked; 10 confirmed, 2 differs, 3 not checked, 1 not applicable

2 fact(s) differ from docs/flood/requirements.md: identifier, nyc_topobathy_2017_resolution_crs_datum. Under FS6 the stage stops until the requirements are corrected.

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FD2. Known biases: The 1 m grid is a patchwork of lidar projects from 2013 to 2025, none from the Ida year; the city product is 1 ft and from 2017, so buildings, grading and drainage changes since then are absent. Bare-earth models remove buildings; hydro-flattening and hydro-enforcement alter water bodies and culverts, which matters for pluvial flooding.

OpenFEMA NFIP Redacted Claims (v3, entity NfipClaims) FEMA, Federal Insurance and Mitigation Administration (OpenFEMA); facts checked: 4 confirmed, 3 read with no claim, 1 not checked; 7 confirmed, 0 differs, 1 not checked, 5 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FT5. Known biases: Only claims on NFIP policies: uninsured, under-insured or out-of-programme losses are missing, and a claim exists only if the owner held a policy and filed. Locations are coarse (0.1 degree, block group) and the dataset is explicitly not an official federal report. Policies cluster in mapped floodplains, so pluvial losses outside them are under-counted.

Facts of OpenFEMA NFIP Redacted Claims (v3, entity NfipClaims). Each fact as read from the primary source on the date shown; claimed is what the requirements say. Facts are not a recomputation of values.

NOAA Atlas 14 Volume 10 Version 3, point precipitation frequency, Jamaica Bay point (40.65, -73.85) NOAA National Weather Service, Office of Water Prediction, Hydrometeorological Design Studies Center (HDSC), Precipitation Frequency Data Server (PFDS); facts checked: 3 confirmed, 7 read with no claim, 1 not checked; 10 confirmed, 0 differs, 1 not checked, 2 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FH6. Known biases: Point estimates only, not areal (the volume says they are not directly applicable to larger areas and an areal reduction factor is needed); estimates assume a stationary climate (historical data); the confidence bounds are 90% intervals and are not symmetric. A reading of intensities against the 1-hour row is for one point and one duration only. Licence text was not found (see licence fact).

NOAA Storm Events Database, bulk CSV files NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), from National Weather Service reports; facts checked: 6 confirmed, 4 read with no claim, 1 differ, 1 not checked; 10 confirmed, 1 differs, 1 not checked, 5 not applicable

1 fact(s) differ from docs/flood/requirements.md: fields. Under FS6 the stage stops until the requirements are corrected.

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FV5, FT5. Known biases: Events are what the National Weather Service office for a county chose to enter, from spotters, public, media, officials and gauges; reporting depends on population, observers and office practice, so a flash flood entry means somebody reported it, and no entry means only that nobody did. Damage fields are estimates and are often 0.00K.

fieldsdiffersfields with unitsDetails file has 51 columns (BEGIN_YEARMONTH ... EVENT_NARRATIVE, DATA_SOURCE); the PDF documents 50 of them and does not describe DATA_SOURCE (value "CSV" in all 136,982 rows of the two files). Units: injuries and deaths in persons; DAMAGE_PROPERTY and DAMAGE_CROPS in dollars as text with K or M suffix ("10.00K = $10,000; 10.00M = $10,000,000"); MAGNITUDE in knots (wind) or inches (hail), not used for floods; BEGIN_RANGE and END_RANGE in miles; TOR_LENGTH miles; TOR_WIDTH yards; coordinates decimal degrees; FLOOD_CAUSE text ("Reported or estimated cause of the flood", e.g. Heavy Rain). Locations file: YEARMONTH, EPISODE_ID, EVENT_ID, LOCATION_INDEX, RANGE, AZIMUTH, LOCATION, LATITUDE, LONGITUDE, LAT2, LON2.https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/swdi/stormevents/csvfiles/Storm-Data-Bulk-csv-Format.pdf

Outcome "differs" is about the documentation, not about requirements.md: the documentation (PDF) and the files disagree in three places. (1) Locations columns are LATITUDE, LONGITUDE, LAT2, LON2 plus YEARMONTH, not lat and lon; LAT2/LON2 look like the same coordinates times 100000 (3817400, 9859400 for 38.29/-98.99, not explained in the PDF). (2) Date-time text in the files is "01-SEP-21 22:00:00" (DD-MON-YY), the PDF shows MM/DD/YYYY. (3) DATA_SOURCE is undocumented. Here it is the publisher's documentation that differs from the publisher's files; the requirements make no claim about the fields.

time_zone furtherconfirmedtime zone handlingTimes are in local standard time of the county or zone ("usually in LST"), with the zone in CZ_TIMEZONE. All 122 rows for the five New York City counties in 2021 and 2023 say EST-5, including events in September when New York is on daylight time, so the text clock is EST (UTC-5), one hour behind the wall clock. 311 Service Requests from 2020 to Present NYC Office of Technology and Innovation (OTI), on NYC Open Data; facts confirmed (10 read with no claim); 12 confirmed, 0 differs, 0 not checked, 1 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FV5, FT5. Known biases: Each row is a call, web or app report made by a person, so counts follow who knows the service and reports, where people are at home or online, and duplicate reports of one event (the dataset has no flag for duplicates). It holds only 'service requests that can be directed to specific agencies'. A report is not a measured flood and says nothing about depth; absence of complaints in an area is not absence of flooding.

Building Elevation and Subgrade (BES) NYC Department of City Planning (DCP), on NYC Open Data; facts confirmed (7 read with no claim); 16 confirmed, 0 differs, 0 not checked, 1 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FD5. Known biases: Everything comes from what a vendor's operators could see in street-level photos and LiDAR from the road: buildings hidden by construction or obstruction (135,503 rows) have estimated grade, 14,039 rows have no measurement (value 0), and subgrade space reachable only from inside (cellars in large buildings) is not recorded, so 'no subgrade' means 'none seen'. Small accessory buildings such as sheds are excluded. The 1,000-row sample fetched is the first 1,000 by BIN and covers Manhattan only.

grade_estimates furtherconfirmedread the guidance note on estimated gradesGrade and floor were read by vendor operators from street-level LiDAR point clouds and photo imagery (captured every 16 feet, March to July 2021 per the dictionary). Where the lowest adjacent grade was below street level or hidden, the value is an estimate from context clues (door or window height); the estimate is flagged only through notes1 ('Property not Visible Due to Construction or Obstruction', 135,503 rows, or 'Property not Visible from Street', 12,082 rows; 147,585 in all), and there is no record of which of grade or floor was estimated. A value of 0 means no measurement: z_grade = 0 in 14,039 rows, z_floor = 0 in 14,038 (14,038 rows have both at 0, one row has z_grade 0 only). The estimated accuracy is called 'reasonable' without a figure.https://data.cityofnewyork.us/api/views/bsin-59hv/files/ae1b369c-6ce1-4805-9ad0-aca9f62f3182

In many instances where the lowest adjacent grade was below street level, the derived measurement in the dataset is an estimate. Any building centroid that has an estimated grade elevation will note “Property not visible due to construction or obstruction” under note_1. Estimates were made by individual data operators based on context clues in the imagery.
[dictionary] While note_1 records if estimates were taken, there is no record of which of the two observed measurements (or both) was the estimated value. DCP has established that the accuracy of estimated spot elevations is reasonable provided that one of the methodologies previously described has been followed.
[dictionary, z_grade] When no measurement has been taken, the field value will be 0

NYC Building Footprints (BUILDING, `5zhs-2jue`) NYC Office of Technology and Innovation (OTI, formerly DoITT), on NYC Open Data; facts checked: 4 confirmed, 3 read with no claim, 1 differ; 7 confirmed, 1 differs, 0 not checked, 1 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F1. Used for FD5. Known biases: Footprints are updated daily by city staff, so the layer is the city as of the download, not as of a storm date; construction_year is reliable only after 2017 and mostly from the tax roll before 2002 (accurate to a decade at best). ground_elevation is a lowest-adjacent-ground value in feet, NAVD88 only for photogrammetric or modern sources, with accuracy that varies; height_roof is zero or null where unavailable. The BIN is not unique (million BINs for unassigned buildings) and a building may be split in several footprints sharing a BIN. Garages (feature code 5110) and other auxiliary structures are in the layer. Numbers in the GeoJSON are strings.

fieldsconfirmedBIN, BBL, construction year, roof height `heightroof`, ground elevation `groundelev`, feature code, last statusThe Socrata table has 16 columns: the_geom, name, bin, doitt_id, shape_area, base_bbl, objectid, construction_year, feature_code, geom_source, ground_elevation, height_roof, last_edited_date, last_status_type, mappluto_bbl, shape_length. The names `heightroof` and `groundelev` are the SHAPEFILE names (HEIGHTROOF, GROUNDELEV); in the Socrata table and the GeoJSON they are `height_roof` and `ground_elevation`. Units: ground_elevation is feet, lowest elevation at the building ground level, NAVD88 when collected photogrammetrically or from modern sources, accuracy varies; height_roof is feet above ground elevation (not above sea level), zero or null means not available. construction_year: year completed, accurate for buildings built after 2017; before 2002 mostly from the tax roll, accurate to a decade at best; null (or 0) means not available. feature_code: 1000 Parking, 1001 Gas Station Canopy, 1002 Storage Tank, 1003 Placeholder (triangle for permitted bldg), 1004 Auxiliary Structure, 1005 Temporary Structure, 1006 Cantilevered Building, 2100 Building, 2110 Skybridge, 5100 Building Under Construction, 5110 Garage. last_status_type: Demolition, Alteration, Geometry, Initialization, Correction, Marked for Construction, Marked For Demolition, Constructed (also seen in the box: Split, Merged, Investigate Construction). bin: DOB building id, first digit borough (1 Manhattan, 2 Bronx, 3 Brooklyn, 4 Queens, 5 Staten Island); BINs ending 000000 (1000000, 3000000 ...) mean unassigned or unknown, so the BIN is not unique. base_bbl: tax lot the footprint lies in (text); mappluto_bbl: the key to join MapPLUTO (condominium billing BBL). doitt_id is the consistent unique building key; objectid is a synthetic key ("Use DOITT_ID instead"). shape_area and shape_length: "Do not use" (Web Mercator, not area preserving). Horizontal: published in WGS84 (GeoJSON), captured in NY State Plane Long Island East, NAD83, US foot (EPSG:2263). In the GeoJSON every property value is a string, numbers included.https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CityOfNewYork/nyc-geo-metadata/master/Metadata/Metadata_BuildingFootprints.md

GROUND_ELEVATION | GROUNDELEV | Lowest elevation at the building ground level, in feet. Calculated from LiDAR or photogrammetrically. | number | Accuracy varies but when collected photogrammetrically or from modern sources this value is based on the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 ; HEIGHT_ROOF | HEIGHTROOF | Roof height above ground elevation, in feet (not above sea level). | number | Records where this is zero or NULL mean that this information was not available. ; BIN ... In some cases where these 6 digits are all zeros (e.g. 1000000, 2000000, etc.) the BIN is unassigned or unknown. ... Due to "million BINs" this identifier is not unique ; FEATURE_CODE | FEAT_CODE | Type of Building. List of values: 1000 = Parking 1001 = Gas Station Canopy ... 5110 = Garage
Features captured: all buildings over 400 sq ft and taller than 12 ft, plus others with BINs; excluded: interior divisions, temporary trailers or tents, jet bridges, awnings, scaffolds, sidewalk sheds, small backyard sheds with no visible car access. Positional accuracy for photogrammetric features +/- 2 ft (95%); manual features less accurate. The ground_elevation datum is stated conditionally (NAVD88 only when collected photogrammetrically or from modern sources): older values may not be NAVD88. The portal's column descriptions for construction_year, feature_code, ground_elevation, height_roof, last_status_type are empty; the meanings come from the GitHub metadata page.

NYC Stormwater Flood Maps NYC Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), published on NYC Open Data; facts checked: 8 confirmed, 4 read with no claim, 2 differ, 1 not checked; values recomputed by a second reader in F2 (passed); 12 confirmed, 2 differs, 1 not checked, 1 not applicable

2 fact(s) differ from docs/flood/requirements.md: min_area_and_depth_rule, depth_classes. Under FS6 the stage stops until the requirements are corrected.

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FS1, FH3. Known biases: Rain-only maps from a model with the drainage system assumed fully working and catch basins clear; parks of 100,000 sq ft or more, non-residential non-commercial lots of 250,000 sq ft or more and lots with railway were masked out, so flooding there is not shown. Areas under 0.25 acre are dropped (with exceptions), and coastal storm surge is not modelled. The publisher says very little observed data on surface flooding exists to check the maps against.

ESRI's shape type carries its curved-segment flag on the class-1 row of the Limited layer and on both rows of the Moderate current layer; the export takes vertices only. Read from the raw shapes: the Limited class-1 row holds one curved segment, about 15 km from the study square, and the Moderate rows none (docs/flood/reports/F2-sources.md, section 1). The geodatabase inner layer name for Moderate 2050 is spelled "..._2_13_per_hr_..." (no "inches"), unlike the others. model furtherconfirmedmodel used **[V]**Hydrologic and hydraulic (H&H) models built in Innovyze InfoWorks ICM: 13 models, one per sewershed draining to a water resource recovery facility, 1D sewer network coupled to a 2D overland mesh (Phase 2), from the City calibrated LTCP models. 10-year scenarios: direct 1D-2D run. 100-year scenario: a composite approach (5-year run, then the remaining 100-year minus 5-year volume placed on the 2D mesh without sewers). Oakwood Beach used rain-on-mesh only. Plan is dated May 2021; the dictionaries only say "hydrologic and hydraulic computer models".https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/orr/pdf/publications/stormwater-resiliency-plan.pdf
passage
The models were built in Innovyze’s InfoWorks ICM software which facilitates coupling of a 1-dimensionsal (1-D) rainfall-runoff and sewer routing component with a 2-dimensional (2D) overland flow and flood visualization component.
Phase 2 modeling developed an H&H model for each hydraulically independent area of the city, resulting in 13 different models
The plan describes the Moderate (10-yr) and Extreme (100-yr) maps. Which approach produced the 1.77 in/hr Limited map is not stated. Whether a given layer used the 1D-2D or the composite approach is stated only for 10-yr and 100-yr.

Known biases: Registry notice of 2026-04-02: about 0.04% of rows were incorrectly masked by brittle pipeline components and the Zarr files were being regenerated; whether corrected data are posted was not found. Checked on 2026-11-25 in F1. Used for FD4. Known biases: None of these is a replacement value of an existing urban substation. MISO and B&V price transmission substations on greenfield, flat, rural assumptions; the California guides price generator interconnection equipment; Con Edison's figures are forecasts for two large indoor New York City substations. Price years differ (2012 or earlier, 2023, 2024, 2025) and some are not stated; figures are reported as stated and are not adjusted. The latest MISO guide (MTEP26, June 2026) keeps its tables in a workbook that was not opened. No distribution (area) substation figure except Con Edison's Idlewild forecast was found.

Facts of Public figures for the replacement or construction cost of electrical substations, by voltage class. Each fact as read from the primary source on the date shown; claimed is what the requirements say. Facts are not a recomputation of values.

Read from the downloaded PDF with pdftotext -layout (f1/cost/miso-mtep24-guide-20240501.pdf). This is the latest MISO guide that prints the substation tables in the PDF. The MTEP25 (redline, March 2025) and MTEP26 (final, June 10 2026; draft March 11 2026) guides no longer print them: they say "All tables referenced in this document are included in MISO's Exploratory Cost Estimate Workbook for MTEP26" and cite the substation tables as Tables 2.4-1 and 2.4-2 and 3.2-1 to 3.2-5 of the workbook; the workbook (xlsx) was not found at any address I could open (the MISO planning pages list no workbook link in their static HTML; the stakeholder page is script-built). So the newest substation figures, MTEP26 in 2026 dollars at +4% escalation from 2025, are NOT checked. No secondary summary is quoted here.

cost_bv_wecc_2012 furtherconfirmedWECC / Black & Veatch "Capital Costs for Transmission and Substations"TITLE: Capital Costs for Transmission and Substations, Recommendations for WECC Transmission Expansion Planning (B&V Project No. 176322). PUBLISHER: Black & Veatch for the Western Electricity Coordinating Council. DATE: October 2012 (the copies read are exhibits: ICNU/201 Mullins in Oregon PUC docket UE 286, filed 2014-07-03, and exhibit PE-22 in a Missouri PSC docket; a later update, February 2014, was not read). ADDRESS READ: the Oregon PUC exhibit PDF (58 pages; the report starts at exhibit page Mullins/1; substation section at PDF pages 38 to 39 and the summary Table 4-2 at PDF page 45), and a 3-page excerpt on the Missouri PSC site. SCOPE: transmission substations at 230, 345, 500 kV (WECC region); no distribution substations. FIGURES AS STATED, columns 230 kV / 345 kV / 500 kV substation. Table 3-1 / 4-2 Base Cost (New Substation): $1,648,000 / $2,060,000 / $2,472,000. Cost Per Line/XFMR Position: $1,442,000 / $2,163,000 / $2,884,000 (Ring Bus Multiplier 1; Breaker and a Half Multiplier 1.5). Transformer cost per MVA: 115/230 kV XFMR $7,000; 138/230 kV $7,000; 230/500 kV $11,000 (in the 230 kV column) ; 115/345 kV $10,000; 138/345 kV $10,000; 230/345 kV $10,000; 345/500 kV $13,000 (345 kV column); 115/500 kV $10,000; 138/500 kV $10,000; 230/500 kV $11,000; 345/500 kV $13,000 (500 kV column). Shunt reactor $20,000 per MVAR (all three); series capacitor $30,000 / $10,000 / $10,000 per MVAR; SVC $85,000 per MVAR; 500 kV HVDC converter station $445,000,000. INCLUDED: the base cost "include[s] land, substation fence, control building, etc" and assumes "flat, barren land with relatively easy site access"; position costs "include the breaker, switches, structures, and protection schemes"; transformer costs "include foundation and oil containment". PRICE YEAR: not stated in the passages read (the report speaks of transmission costs "escalated from the original 2008 values" for one table); the report is dated October 2012. To build a substation of N positions the report's method is base cost plus N positions plus transformers; no total is printed.https://edocs.puc.state.or.us/efdocs/HTB/ue286htb14453.pdf
