cost_coned_idlewild_2023 furtherconfirmedNY Consolidated Edison rate-case or PSC material with a stated substation costTITLE: Petition of Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. for Authorization and Cost Recovery for the Reliable Clean City - Idlewild Project, NY PSC Case 22-E-0064. PUBLISHER: Con Edison, filed with the New York Public Service Commission, August 22, 2023. ADDRESS READ: the DPS document system link above. SCOPE: both. A new 138 kV TRANSMISSION substation and a new 27 kV DISTRIBUTION AREA substation, in Queens, New York City. FIGURES AS STATED: "Con Edison forecasts the total capital cost of the Project to be approximately $1.2 billion broken downs as follows: approximately $592 million for the Eastern Queens Transmission Substation; approximately $380 million for the Idlewild Distribution Area Substation; and approximately $242 million for electric facilities, e.g., feeders, for the new Springfield Network." The funding annex states "The funding request is based on order of magnitude estimates" with, in $000s: Eastern Queens $592,105; Idlewild Area Substation $380,127; Jamaica Network Split (Springfield) $242,066; Total Project Cost (including 2028) $1,214,298. DESCRIPTION: Eastern Queens is "an indoor, 138kV, gas insulated switchgear substation arranged in a double ring bus configuration" with circuit breakers and four 138 kV connections, expandable to five, and the re-routing of existing feeders 903 and 901 L and M; Idlewild is "an indoor, 27 kV substation arranged in a double synchronous bus configuration" with four 93 MVA, 138 kV/27 kV transformers (provision for a fifth), fifty feeder positions (seventeen new 27 kV feeders). Both co-located on a vacant company-owned parcel in Jamaica, Queens. In-service April 2028 (Eastern Queens) and May 2028 (Idlewild). PRICE YEAR: not stated in the passages read; the funding request is by year 2023 to 2028 and the "Total Project Cost (including 2028)" is a sum over the years (nominal or not is not stated).https://documents.dps.ny.gov/public/Common/ViewDoc.aspx?DocRefId=%7BB0B81E8A-0100-CC67-8F61-5E885C254A5A%7D

These are utility forecasts for two large indoor gas-insulated and four-transformer facilities, well above the MISO table range: an upper bound on a New York City installation, not a typical area substation. Other New York figures seen only as search-engine snippets and NOT checked (not opened): a $47.3 million Parkchester No. 1 fifth transformer approval in the Bronx (2025 trade press), and a $1.3 billion package including a Sunset Park 345 kV substation in Brooklyn. The Con Edison marginal cost study and the NYISO studies were not read. The area-substation counts and voltages in the Con Edison 2013-era testimony were not read.

Known biases: Curves F2.1 to F2.3 (substations) are identical for the three voltage classes and stop at 3.05 m depth with damage factor 0.16; there are no values above 3.05 m although the sheet's depth column runs to 6.5 m, so a table to a deeper maximum would need an extrapolation or cap rule that is not in the source. Williams et al. 2025; Bor et al. 2026; Karagiannakis et al. 2025 Journal of Flood Risk Management (Wiley); arXiv; WIREs Climate Change (Wiley); facts checked: 6 confirmed, 6 read with no claim, 1 not checked; 12 confirmed, 0 differs, 1 not checked, 4 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FR2. Known biases: Williams: the full text was not readable (Wiley returns HTTP 403 to automated clients and no open copy was found), so its numbers are unchecked; it is a New Zealand expert-elicitation study. Bor et al. is a preprint (manuscript submitted to Earth's Future), not peer reviewed, and Table 1 gives HV (>345 kV, anchored) substations only; the flood parameters are taken from a literature synthesis (Kabre and Weimar 2022). Karagiannakis was read on an arXiv copy of the article, not the publisher page.

Facts of Williams et al. 2025; Bor et al. 2026; Karagiannakis et al. 2025. Each fact as read from the primary source on the date shown; claimed is what the requirements say. Facts are not a recomputation of values.

A threshold of almost 1.2 m, representing 7% equipment damage, is applied to all classes. The damage percentage increases to 15% at the maximum considered flooding depth of approximately 3 m (the depth is measured from ground level, assuming that equipment is located about 0.91 m above ground).
Secondary copy of the article (arXiv, arXiv API says arxiv:doi 10.1002/wcc.930).

National Structure Inventory (NSI) 2026 Base U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (NSI development team); facts checked: 4 confirmed, 7 read with no claim, 1 not checked; 11 confirmed, 0 differs, 1 not checked, 1 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FD5. Known biases: A modeled inventory, not a survey: attributes are estimated from parcels, footprints, Census data and regional distributions, so foundation height, basement and values are typical rather than measured. Prices are August 2025, the inventory reflects roughly 2025 buildings and population, and stacked structures are counted as several records on one footprint.

Facts of National Structure Inventory (NSI) 2026 Base. Each fact as read from the primary source on the date shown; claimed is what the requirements say. Facts are not a recomputation of values.

fieldsconfirmedoccupancy type, foundation type or basement, first-floor height found_ht, replacement value val_struct, stories, ground elevationAll present in the public 2026 schema and in my sample: occtype (e.g. RES3C, COM4; Hazus-style damage function name), st_damcat (RES/COM/IND/PUB), found_type (C crawl, B basement, S slab, P pier, I pile, F fill, W solid wall), found_ht ("foundation height of the structure in feet from the ground elevation"), num_story, val_struct (depreciated replacement value in dollars), val_cont, val_vehic, fullrep (full non-depreciated replacement value, new in 2026), depindex, sqft, ftprntsqft, bldheight (metres), ground_elv (feet, NAVD88) and grnd_elv_m (metres, NAVD88), med_yr_blt (median of the census tract, not the building), firmzone, zone_sub, static_bfe, x/y WGS84. A basement is only the found_type=B flag: the detailed `basement` field (finished/unfinished/none) is a restricted field for federal users and mission partners. Statistics are mine (scripts analyse_f1.py, nsi_county.py in f1/scripts). The st_damcat classes and the occtype letters disagree (occtype REL, EDU, GOV fall under PUB in st_damcat, as inferred from the counts; not read from the documentation). found_ht takes only four values and is 2 ft for 76% of records, which looks like assignment from foundation-type rules, not measurement (same observation as in the F0 sample). The study's Brooklyn buildings are those with cbfips starting 36047; the box also returns 1,444 Manhattan records.
join_fields_to_city_buildings furtherconfirmedwhich identifier fields could join it to the city's buildingsThere is no BIN, BBL or DOITT id in the 42 fields. What exists: (1) x, y: WGS84 longitude and latitude of the structure point (all inside the box; the structure is placed at the footprint or parcel centroid), so the join to city footprints or BES centroids is spatial (point in polygon, or nearest); (2) fd_id: integer, unique per record (22,896 distinct), the NSI's own record key; (3) bid: text built on an Open Location Code (plus code) of the footprint plus suffixes, for example "87G8M2RX+Q8H-3-4-3-4", filled in 11,596 records, empty ("") in the others; (4) ftprntid: footprint id, either "none_<number>" (11,300 records) or "<county FIPS>_<number>" such as "36047_158616" (5,647 distinct values over the other 11,596 records, so several records share a footprint: stacked structures); (5) usastrucid: filled in 9,744 records (for example "7913338"), empty in the others; (6) cbfips: 15-digit Census 2020 block id; (7) ftprntsrc: footprint source (P 11,280; NGA 9,657; Bing 1,852; ORNL 87; H 20). None of the ids was matched to a city id here.https://nsi.sec.usace.army.mil/nsiapi/structures?bbox=-73.9900,40.6850,-73.9900,40.7245,-73.9385,40.7245,-73.9385,40.6850,-73.9900,40.6850

USGS 3DEP 1 m DEM tiles over the F1 study box (north Brooklyn, 500 m margin) U.S. Geological Survey, 3D Elevation Program; facts confirmed (3 read with no claim); 13 confirmed, 0 differs, 0 not checked, 2 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F1. Used for FD2, FH2. Known biases: Bare-earth model from 2013-14 lidar: buildings, grading, drainage and shoreline changes since then are absent. Water is hydro-flattened (a flat surface, here at -1.62 m), so water depth and channel shape are not terrain. Elevations are NAD83/NAVD88 metres; the tile CRS is EPSG:26918 (NAD83), the project CRS EPSG:32618 (WGS84); the two differ by about a metre at most and the numbers were used unchanged. Flight dates are a project range, not per-flight dates.

Geospatial datasets of water surface elevation and water depth in New York City associated with the remnants of Hurricane Ida, September 1, 2021 U.S. Geological Survey, New York Water Science Center (via ScienceBase); facts checked: 2 confirmed, 11 read with no claim, 1 not checked; 13 confirmed, 0 differs, 1 not checked, 0 not applicable

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FV1. Known biases: Covers only discs of 250 m radius around 83 surveyed marks; everywhere else there is no depth. The depth is the mark minus lidar ground, assuming flat water, so it is derived from the marks and not an independent observation. Drains and subway spaces are ignored and the lidar is 2017, four years before the event.

what_the_depth_is furtherread, no claim–NOT a hydrodynamic model. Depth = surveyed HWM elevation minus lidar ground elevation, within a 250 m circle around each mark, assuming a single constant water surface across that circle, connected low ground only, ground more than 1 ft below the mark treated as flowing water and removed. Sinks (subways, storm drains) ignored. Buildings inundated only if z_floor <= water level and the building has a subgrade space.https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/file/get/63badf22d34e92aad3cd279e?f=__disk__74%2F82%2F91%2F74829135b81999cf615c9a3416efcb9003c0de8f
passage
"These depth maps assume a constant water-surface elevation across the landscape around each HWM and show where potential inundation may have occurred during the rainfall event." ; "1) The extent of inundation was limited by the land-surface elevation within a 250-meter distance buffer around each HWM location." ; "5) All potential sinks were ignored."
For validation this means the raster at a mark is almost a restatement of that mark (depth = mark minus lidar); it is not an independent observation away from the marks.

USGS high-water marks for the remnants of Hurricane Ida, five boroughs of New York City U.S. Geological Survey, New York Water Science Center (via ScienceBase); facts checked: 6 confirmed, 5 read with no claim, 1 differ, 2 not checked; values to be recomputed by a second reader in F5; 11 confirmed, 1 differs, 2 not checked, 0 not applicable

1 fact(s) differ from docs/flood/requirements.md: mark_count. Under FS6 the stage stops until the requirements are corrected.

Checked on 2026-11-25 in F0. Used for FV1. Known biases: Marks exist only where crews found and surveyed debris, mud or seed lines, up to 2.5 months after the event, in the five boroughs (159 marks at 83 sites; 54 sites in Brooklyn and Queens). Areas without such evidence, and basements and subway spaces, are not represented. Horizontal positions are map or phone fixes (WGS84 from digital map), and the whole set is tagged "Riverine" and mostly "swift water" although the event was pluvial.

Facts of USGS high-water marks for the remnants of Hurricane Ida, five boroughs of New York City. Each fact as read from the primary source on the date shown; claimed is what the requirements say. Facts are not a recomputation of values.
